specPoints.text: understand the reactions of alcohols with: i oxygen in air (combustion) ii halogenating agents: • PCl 5 to produce chloroalkanes (including its use as a qualitative test for the presence of the –OH group) • 50% concentrated sulfuric acid and potassium bromide to produce bromoalkanes • red phosphorus and iodine to produce iodoalkanes iii concentrated phosphoric acid to form alkenes by elimination Descriptions of the mechanisms of these reactions are not required.

primer.text: Alcohols burn, swap their hydroxyl for every halogen, and dehydrate to alkenes. This note balances the combustion equation, routes chlorination through PCl5 or acid, bromination through in-situ HBr, iodination through PI3, and shows how concentrated phosphoric acid squeezes out water to close a double bond.

lessons.title: Combustion: alcohols as fuels
lessons.opening: Ignited in air, alcohols burn just as hydrocarbons do, releasing carbon dioxide and water. This lesson writes the combustion word equation, balances representative cases, and notes why the alcohols' clean, energy-rich burning makes them practical fuels.
keyPoints: Ignited in air, alcohols burn in oxygen and undergo complete combustion.
The products of complete combustion are carbon dioxide and water, matching the hydrocarbon pattern.
The word equation is alcohol plus oxygen giving carbon dioxide plus water.
Longer-chain alcohols carry more carbon per molecule, so their complete combustion equations need proportionally more oxygen.
The reaction is strongly exothermic, which underlies the use of alcohols such as ethanol as fuels.

low.restatement: Burn the alcohol completely and every carbon becomes carbon dioxide while every hydrogen becomes water; count the atoms on each side to fix the oxygen coefficient.
low.analogy: Burning is an auction where carbon and hydrogen bid for oxygen atoms - balancing pays each atom exactly what it needs and nothing more.
low.examPointer: Balance combustion equations by counting carbons first, then hydrogens, then oxygen last; state the products as carbon dioxide and water for complete burning.

medium.restatement: Complete combustion means oxygen is plentiful, so no carbon monoxide or soot forms; the atom census on both sides of the equation must close exactly, which is why the oxygen coefficient grows with chain length.
medium.analogy: A busy restaurant kitchen: every plate (carbon and hydrogen) must leave with its exact order of oxygen sides; short orders need less oxygen, long orders more.
medium.examPointer: Quote the balanced equation for the named alcohol and flag the reaction as exothermic when a question asks why alcohols serve as fuels.

check.stem: Which products form when an alcohol burns completely in air?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water only
options.explanation: Complete combustion converts all carbon to CO2 and all hydrogen to H2O.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide signals incomplete combustion with limited oxygen.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: Hydrogen burns to water; it is not a combustion product of the alcohol.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water and soot
options.explanation: Soot indicates incomplete combustion, not the complete case.

check.stem: Complete combustion of methanol requires how many oxygen molecules per methanol molecule?

options.text: One and a half, giving 2CH3OH + 3O2 in whole-number form
options.explanation: CH3OH + 1.5O2 closes the census: one carbon, four hydrogens, four oxygens each side.

options.text: One
options.explanation: One oxygen molecule cannot oxidise all four hydrogens to water and the carbon to carbon dioxide.

options.text: Two
options.explanation: Two oxygen molecules over-supplies the census by one oxygen.

options.text: Three per methanol molecule
options.explanation: That would give six oxygens per methanol, double the requirement.

check.stem: Why are alcohols useful as fuels?

options.text: Their combustion is strongly exothermic and, when complete, gives clean products
options.explanation: Energy release plus simple products underlie the fuel use of ethanol and methanol.

options.text: They burn without needing any oxygen
options.explanation: Combustion requires oxygen; no fuel burns without it.

options.text: They are non-flammable liquids
options.explanation: Alcohols are flammable; that is the basis of their fuel role.

options.text: They produce carbon monoxide as their main product
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide is the incomplete-combustion product and a hazard, not the goal.

check.stem: Compared with methanol, the complete combustion of propan-1-ol needs

options.text: More oxygen per molecule, because three carbons and eight hydrogens demand more oxidation
options.explanation: More atoms per molecule means a larger oxygen coefficient in the balanced equation.

options.text: The same oxygen per molecule, since all alcohols burn alike
options.explanation: Atom counts differ, so the oxygen demands differ.

options.text: Less oxygen, because the alcohol supplies its own oxygen atom
options.explanation: The single hydroxyl oxygen is far short of the demand from three carbons.

options.text: No oxygen at all, since alcohols self-oxidise
options.explanation: Air supplies the oxidant; the alcohol does not oxidise itself.

check.stem: A yellow, sooty flame during an alcohol's burning indicates

options.text: Incomplete combustion, with insufficient oxygen producing soot and possibly carbon monoxide
options.explanation: Soot is unburnt carbon, the classic sign that oxygen supply fell short.

options.text: Complete combustion at a higher temperature
options.explanation: Complete burning gives a clean blue flame without soot.

options.text: That the alcohol has a longer carbon chain than expected
options.explanation: Chain length changes the oxygen demand but not the flame colour when oxygen is ample.

options.text: Water condensing on the flame
options.explanation: Condensed water is invisible; soot is the combustion signature.

check.stem: State the word equation for the complete combustion of an alcohol.
check.modelAnswer: Alcohol plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water, with the oxygen supplied from the air.

check.stem: Name the two products of complete combustion and the condition they require.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water form when oxygen is plentiful enough for complete burning.

check.stem: Explain why the alcohol's own oxygen atom does not make its combustion oxygen requirement zero.
check.modelAnswer: One hydroxyl oxygen cannot cover the many oxygen atoms needed to oxidise every carbon to carbon dioxide and every hydrogen to water, so air must still supply the balance of the oxygen demand.

check.stem: Balance the complete combustion of ethanol in molecular form and verify the atom census.
check.modelAnswer: C2H5OH + 3O2 gives 2CO2 + 3H2O: carbon census 2 = 2, hydrogen census 6 = 6, oxygen census 1 + 6 = 7 on the left and 4 + 3 = 7 on the right, so the equation closes exactly.

lessons.title: Swapping -OH for a halogen: three routes
lessons.opening: Each halogen has its own reagent for replacing the hydroxyl group. Chlorine arrives through phosphorus(V) chloride or, for tertiary alcohols, concentrated hydrochloric acid; bromine rides in via hydrogen bromide made in situ; iodine through phosphorus and iodine under reflux. This lesson maps all three routes and their tell-tale observations.
keyPoints: Conversions to halogenoalkanes replace the hydroxyl group with a halogen atom, a change known as halogenation.
Phosphorus(V) chloride reacts vigorously with alcohols at room temperature, releasing steamy HCl fumes.
The PCl5 reaction doubles as a qualitative test for the -OH group via its steaming fumes.
Tertiary alcohols can also be chlorinated by shaking with concentrated hydrochloric acid alone, a route closed to primary and secondary alcohols.
Bromination uses potassium bromide with 50 percent sulfuric acid to generate HBr in situ, and iodination uses red phosphorus plus iodine under reflux via PI3.

low.restatement: Pick the reagent by halogen: PCl5 for a fast room-temperature chloride with steamy fumes, KBr plus half-strength sulfuric acid for the bromide, red phosphorus and iodine under reflux for the iodide; each route swaps the hydroxyl for the halogen.
low.analogy: Three courier services deliver one parcel: same replacement job, different vehicles and timetables - PCl5 same-day, HBr warmed, PI3 reflux.
low.examPointer: Match reagent to halogen in answers and quote the steamy-fumes test when asked how to confirm an -OH group.

medium.restatement: The in-situ routes make the hydrogen halide first - sulfate or phosphorus chemistry manufactures HBr or PI3 - and the hydrogen halide then does the substitution; the tertiary route works by a different, acid-catalysed pathway that primary and secondary carbons cannot support.
medium.analogy: Build the delivery van before the parcel can ship: the inorganic pre-reaction manufactures the actual substituting agent for bromine and iodine.
medium.examPointer: Write the two-step inorganic-then-substitution equations for bromination and iodination, and restrict the direct HCl route to tertiary alcohols.

check.stem: What is observed when phosphorus(V) chloride is added to an unknown alcohol?

options.text: A vigorous reaction at room temperature releasing steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride
options.explanation: The -OH group is replaced and HCl gas escapes as misty fumes, confirming the hydroxyl group.

options.text: A slow reaction only after prolonged heating
options.explanation: The PCl5 reaction is vigorous at room temperature with no heating needed.

options.text: A red precipitate forming slowly
options.explanation: No precipitate forms; the diagnostic observation is the fumes.

options.text: A blue flame as the alcohol ignites
options.explanation: PCl5 addition does not ignite the mixture.

check.stem: Why can concentrated hydrochloric acid alone chlorinate a tertiary alcohol but not a primary one?

options.text: The tertiary pathway proceeds by a different mechanism that primary carbons cannot support
options.explanation: Tertiary carbocations are accessible for the acid route, while primary carbons lack that pathway.

options.text: Primary alcohols are too volatile for the acid route
options.explanation: Volatility is irrelevant to the mechanistic reach of the acid route.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid is too weak for any alcohol
options.explanation: The acid does chlorinate tertiary alcohols, so the acid strength is sufficient there.

options.text: Primary alcohols lack a hydroxyl group
options.explanation: Primary alcohols carry the same -OH group as tertiary ones.

check.stem: In the bromination of an alcohol, the 50 percent sulfuric acid concentration matters because

options.text: Stronger acid would oxidise bromide ions to bromine, diverting the route into side products
options.explanation: Half-strength acid generates HBr cleanly; full strength sends bromide off to Br2.

options.text: Weaker acid would evaporate the potassium bromide
options.explanation: Evaporation is not the concern; bromide oxidation is.

options.text: The acid acts as the bromine source itself
options.explanation: The bromine comes from KBr; the acid generates HBr from it.

options.text: The acid catalyses the alcohol's dehydration instead
options.explanation: Dehydration is the phosphoric acid route, not this one.

check.stem: The iodination of an alcohol requires heating under reflux because

options.text: The phosphorus-plus-iodine route is slow, so prolonged heating with everything retained is needed
options.explanation: Reflux keeps the volatile species in the mixture while the substitution crawls to completion.

options.text: Iodine gas escapes unless the condenser blocks it permanently
options.explanation: Reflux does retain volatiles, but the reason is the slow reaction needing sustained heating.

options.text: The alcohol would freeze at room temperature
options.explanation: Alcohols are liquids at room temperature; freezing is not the issue.

options.text: PI3 reacts instantly and no heating is ever used
options.explanation: The route explicitly requires heating under reflux.

check.stem: Which inorganic compound forms as a co-product when phosphorus(III) iodide reacts with an alcohol?

options.text: Phosphorous acid, H3PO3
options.explanation: The substitution hands the three iodine atoms to alcohol molecules and the phosphorus emerges as H3PO3.

options.text: Phosphoric acid, H3PO4
options.explanation: Phosphoric acid is the dehydration reagent, not this co-product.

options.text: Phosphorus(V) chloride
options.explanation: PCl5 belongs to the chlorination route entirely.

options.text: Potassium sulfate
options.explanation: Potassium sulfate is the bromination pre-reaction co-product.

check.stem: State the observation that identifies the -OH group using phosphorus(V) chloride.
check.modelAnswer: Steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride are released immediately at room temperature, evidencing the hydroxyl group.

check.stem: Name the reagents used to supply bromine and iodine in the alcohol conversions.
check.modelAnswer: Bromination uses potassium bromide with 50 percent sulfuric acid, and iodination uses red phosphorus with iodine under reflux.

check.stem: Explain why the bromination reaction is written as two separate equations.
check.modelAnswer: The inorganic reagents react together first to make hydrogen bromide and potassium sulfate, and only then does the hydrogen bromide substitute the alcohol's hydroxyl group, so the chemistry splits into a generation step and a substitution step.

check.stem: Write the two-step equations for converting butan-1-ol to 1-bromobutane and verify the atom census of the second step.
check.modelAnswer: Step one is 2KBr + H2SO4 giving K2SO4 + 2HBr; step two is CH3CH2CH2CH2OH + HBr giving CH3CH2CH2CH2Br + H2O, whose census closes with four carbons, ten hydrogens and one oxygen on each side.

lessons.title: Dehydration: squeezing water out to make alkenes
lessons.opening: Heated with concentrated phosphoric acid, an alcohol loses water across adjacent carbons and forms an alkene. This lesson shows the elimination pattern, writes the ethanol case, and explains why the acid never appears in the equation.
keyPoints: Dehydration heats the alcohol with concentrated phosphoric acid to remove water and form a C=C bond.
The reaction mirrors the elimination chemistry of halogenoalkanes, removing OH and an adjacent hydrogen.
The ethanol case is CH3CH2OH giving CH2=CH2 and water.
The C=C double bond forms between the carbon that lost the hydroxyl and its hydrogen-bearing neighbour.
The equation omits the phosphoric acid because the water formed dilutes the concentrated reagent.

low.restatement: Heat the alcohol in concentrated phosphoric acid: the hydroxyl and a neighbouring hydrogen leave together as water, their carbons bond double, and an alkene emerges.
low.analogy: Two seats on a bus vacated together let the remaining passengers link arms across the gap - the departing water frees the carbons to join as C=C.
low.examPointer: Write the alcohol-to-alkene equation with water as the co-product and state the catalyst's dilution when asked why it is absent.

medium.restatement: Elimination needs a leaving group and a beta hydrogen; the acid protonates the hydroxyl, water departs, and the adjacent hydrogen's electrons swing in to close the double bond. The freshly formed water dilutes the acid, so the catalyst works by contact rather than stoichiometrically.
medium.analogy: A talent show where the host (the acid) coaxes one act (water) off stage, letting the two neighbouring acts link their performance into one double act.
medium.examPointer: Connect dehydration to halogenoalkane elimination when comparing elimination chemistry, and name concentrated phosphoric acid as the reagent of choice.

check.stem: Which reagent dehydrates an alcohol to an alkene?

options.text: Concentrated phosphoric acid
options.explanation: Heating with concentrated H3PO4 removes water and forms the alkene.

options.text: Phosphorus(V) chloride
options.explanation: PCl5 substitutes the hydroxyl with chlorine rather than eliminating water.

options.text: Sodium carbonate solution
options.explanation: Carbonate washes products; it does not dehydrate alcohols.

options.text: Dilute sulfuric acid at room temperature
options.explanation: The dehydration reagent is concentrated phosphoric acid with heating.

check.stem: What bonds form during the dehydration of an alcohol?

options.text: A carbon-carbon double bond between the hydroxyl carbon and its neighbour
options.explanation: Eliminating water lets the adjacent carbons close into a C=C bond.

options.text: A carbon-oxygen double bond in place of the hydroxyl
options.explanation: The oxygen leaves with the water; no C=O forms in alkene products.

options.text: A carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: Halogenation forms C-X; dehydration forms C=C.

options.text: An oxygen-oxygen bond
options.explanation: No peroxide chemistry is involved in dehydration.

check.stem: Why does concentrated phosphoric acid not appear in the dehydration equation?

options.text: The water formed in the reaction dilutes the concentrated acid, so the catalyst is not consumed into the stoichiometry
options.explanation: The acid serves as the dehydrating medium while the product water dilutes it.

options.text: The acid evaporates before the reaction starts
options.explanation: Phosphoric acid is not the volatile component here.

options.text: The acid is insoluble in alcohols
options.explanation: Catalysts need not dissolve; the real reason is dilution by the product water.

options.text: The acid is reduced to phosphorus during the reaction
options.explanation: No redox change befalls the acid in dehydration.

check.stem: The dehydration of ethanol produces which alkene?

options.text: Ethene, CH2=CH2
options.explanation: Losing water from ethanol closes a double bond between the two carbons, giving ethene.

options.text: Ethenol, with the OH still attached
options.explanation: The hydroxyl group is removed in dehydration; it cannot remain.

options.text: Ethyne, with a triple bond
options.explanation: One elimination forms a double bond, not a triple bond.

options.text: Ethane, by reduction
options.explanation: Dehydration is elimination, not reduction; no hydrogen is added.

check.stem: Dehydration of an alcohol is described as similar to the elimination reaction of a halogenoalkanes because both

options.text: Remove a small molecule across adjacent carbons to leave a C=C double bond
options.explanation: Halogenoalkanes eliminate HX and alcohols eliminate water, both closing the double bond.

options.text: Require a halogen atom to depart
options.explanation: Alcohol dehydration departs water, with no halogen involved.

options.text: Produce alcohols as their products
options.explanation: Both produce alkenes, not alcohols.

options.text: Occur only at room temperature
options.explanation: Both eliminations need heating to proceed.

check.stem: State the equation for the dehydration of ethanol.
check.modelAnswer: CH3CH2OH gives CH2=CH2 and H2O when heated with concentrated phosphoric acid.

check.stem: Name the bonds broken and formed when an alcohol dehydrates.
check.modelAnswer: The C-O bond of the hydroxyl and a C-H bond on the adjacent carbon break, while a C=C double bond forms between those carbons.

check.stem: Explain why the water formed in dehydration is the molecule that dilutes the acid.
check.modelAnswer: The eliminated hydroxyl and adjacent hydrogen combine into exactly the water that appears as the co-product, and that fresh water mixes into and dilutes the concentrated phosphoric acid as the reaction proceeds.

check.stem: Predict the alkene products when butan-2-ol dehydrates and justify why more than one alkene can form.
check.modelAnswer: The hydroxyl carbon can pair its elimination with hydrogens on either neighbouring carbon, so but-1-ene and but-2-ene both form, with the double bond closing on whichever side loses the hydrogen.

glossary.definition: Burning with ample oxygen so that all carbon becomes carbon dioxide and all hydrogen becomes water.
Replacement of an alcohol's hydroxyl group by a halogen atom to form a halogenoalkane.
Elimination of water from an alcohol using concentrated phosphoric acid to form an alkene.

workedExample.prompt: Verify the two-step bromination chemistry: the inorganic generation step 2KBr + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2HBr, then the substitution CH3CH2CH2CH2OH + HBr -> CH3CH2CH2CH2Br + H2O.
steps: Census the generation step: potassium 2 = 2, bromine 2 = 2, hydrogen 2 = 2, sulfur 1 = 1, oxygen 4 = 4, so the first equation closes.
Census the substitution step's carbons: 4 = 4, and its bromines: 1 = 1.
Census the substitution step's hydrogens: 9 + 1 on the left against 9 + 2 on the right, totalling 10 = 10.
Census oxygen: 1 = 1, so every atom book balances across both steps.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Both equations balance exactly: the HBr is generated in situ and then substitutes the hydroxyl of butan-1-ol without any atom deficit.
